title: Eulerian Paths in Directed Graphs
description: Extends the Eulerian circuit characterization to directed graphs. A weakly connected digraph has an Eulerian circuit iff every vertex has equal in-degree and out-degree; it has an Eulerian path from s to t iff outdeg(s)=indeg(s)+1, indeg(t)=outdeg(t)+1, and all other vertices are balanced. The directed handshaking lemma (∑ outDeg = |E| = ∑ inDeg) and necessity direction (Eulerian circuit → balanced) are proved from first principles. 12 theorems proved, 2 axioms (Hierholzer sufficiency and path characterization).

overview.historicalContext:
Euler's 1736 paper 'Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis' on the Königsberg bridges introduced graph theory and proved the necessity direction of the Eulerian theorem for undirected graphs: an Eulerian circuit exists only if every vertex has even degree. The directed analogue emerged naturally: in a directed graph (digraph), an Eulerian circuit requires that each vertex has equal in-degree and out-degree — one outgoing edge consumed for each incoming edge at every visit. **Hierholzer's algorithm** (1873) proved sufficiency constructively: start any closed walk; if edges remain, splice in subcircuits at the first repeated vertex. The algorithm runs in O(|E|) and directly applies to directed graphs with the same degree balance condition.

The theory gained surprising new depth with **de Bruijn sequences** (Nicolaas de Bruijn, 1946). A de Bruijn sequence of order n over alphabet Σ is a cyclic sequence in which every length-n string over Σ appears exactly once. De Bruijn (and independently Good, 1946) observed that such sequences correspond to **Eulerian circuits in de Bruijn graphs**: vertices are length-(n-1) words, edges are length-n words, with the edge $(w_1\ldots w_{n-1})\to(w_2\ldots w_n)$ representing the word $w_1\ldots w_n$. The de Bruijn graph is regular (each vertex has in-degree = out-degree = |Σ|), so Eulerian circuits always exist, proving de Bruijn sequences always exist and giving an efficient construction via Hierholzer's algorithm.

The **BEST theorem** (van Aardenne-Ehrenfest and de Bruijn 1951; Smith and Tutte 1941–1948) counts Eulerian circuits in directed graphs: the number of distinct Eulerian circuits starting at vertex $w$ is $t_w(G) \times \prod_{v} (\text{outDeg}(v)-1)!$, where $t_w(G)$ is the number of arborescences (spanning directed trees rooted at $w$). This remarkable formula connects Eulerian counting to the Matrix-Tree theorem.

In computational biology, **Eulerian path algorithms on de Bruijn graphs** became the basis for next-generation sequencing assembly. Pevzner, Tang, and Waterman (2001) introduced the EULER assembler: decompose a genome into overlapping k-mers, construct the de Bruijn graph, and find an Eulerian path. The genome is the sequence spelled by the Eulerian path — a dramatic application of 18th-century graph theory to 21st-century genomics.
overview.problemStatement: Extend the Eulerian circuit characterization (from undirected graphs) to directed graphs: characterize when a directed graph has an Eulerian circuit or path in terms of in-degrees and out-degrees.
overview.text: For a weakly connected directed graph G: (1) G has an Eulerian circuit iff every vertex v satisfies inDeg(v) = outDeg(v). (2) G has an Eulerian path from s to t (s≠t) iff outDeg(s)=inDeg(s)+1, inDeg(t)=outDeg(t)+1, and all other vertices v have inDeg(v)=outDeg(v).
overview.proofStrategy: Define DiGraph V as a Finset of directed edges with no self-loops. Define outDegree and inDegree by filtering edges. Prove the directed handshaking lemma (∑ outDeg = |E| = ∑ inDeg) from first principles via double-counting: swap ∑_v and ∑_e using Finset.sum_comm, then apply Finset.sum_ite_eq'. Prove necessity (HasEulerianCircuit → IsEulerianBalanced) via a walk-position bijection argument: use the unique-coverage property to biject edges with walk positions, then show source-count = target-count using the closed walk property (walk[0] = walk[n] implies a circular shift bijection). Axiomatize the remaining directions (Hierholzer sufficiency, path characterization). Verify concrete examples (directed triangle, directed path) by native_decide.
keyInsights: The directed handshaking lemma is proved by Finset.sum_comm: ∑_v |{e : e.1=v}| = ∑_e ∑_v [e.1=v] = ∑_e 1 = |E|. No Finset.card_biUnion needed.

Necessity requires a bijection between G.edges and walk positions. The key insight is to strengthen HasEulerianCircuit with ∃! (unique position per edge) and an hsteps condition (every walk step is an edge), enabling use of ExistsUnique.unique for injectivity.

The closed walk balance is proved by a bijection i ↦ (i=0 ? n-1 : i-1) from source positions {i < n : walk[i] = v} to target positions {i < n : walk[i+1] = v}, using the closed walk condition walk[0] = walk[n].
The directed triangle A→B→C→A is the canonical Eulerian circuit example: all three vertices have in-degree = out-degree = 1, verified by native_decide over Fin 3.

For the Eulerian path characterization, the source s has one more outgoing edge than incoming (to start the path), and the sink t has one more incoming edge than outgoing (to end the path). All intermediate vertices are balanced.
Weak connectivity (underlying undirected graph is connected) is the correct connectivity notion for directed Eulerian theory — strong connectivity is not required for the equivalence.

De Bruijn sequence connection: the de Bruijn graph B(n, Σ) is a digraph on length-(n-1) strings where each vertex has in-degree = out-degree = |Σ|. The directed Eulerian theorem guarantees Eulerian circuits exist in any such balanced weakly-connected digraph, proving de Bruijn sequences of every order exist over every alphabet — and Hierholzer's algorithm constructs them in O(|Σ|^n) time.

BEST theorem: the number of Eulerian circuits starting at vertex w in a directed Eulerian graph equals t_w(G) × ∏_v (outDeg(v)-1)!, where t_w(G) is the number of arborescences (spanning in-trees) rooted at w. This connects Eulerian circuit counting to the Matrix-Tree theorem (Kirchhoff 1847) — a deep result in algebraic graph theory.

Flow conservation interpretation: the directed handshaking equality ∑ outDeg = ∑ inDeg is equivalent to Kirchhoff's current law (KCL) in electrical networks and conservation of flow in network flow problems. An Eulerian graph (every vertex balanced) is one where a unit of 'flow' entering each vertex also leaves — the combinatorial version of a conservative vector field.

Eulerian vs Hamiltonian — the algorithmic complexity contrast: deciding whether a directed graph has an Eulerian circuit is solvable in O(|V|+|E|) time (check balance + weak connectivity, both linear-time); deciding whether it has a Hamiltonian circuit is NP-complete (Karp 1972, one of the 21 original NP-complete problems). The degree-balance characterization formalized here, by reducing the global existence question to a vertex-local arithmetic invariant ∀v, inDeg(v) = outDeg(v), is the source of the polynomial-time gap — the analogous reduction for Hamiltonian circuits fails (no comparable local invariant exists), explaining why Eulerian paths became the basis for modern genome assembly (Pevzner-Tang-Waterman 2001) while Hamiltonian-path assembly was abandoned.

Generalization to hypergraphs and infinite graphs: the directed Eulerian theorem here is the r=2 (binary edges), finite case of a much broader phenomenon. For r-uniform hypergraphs (r≥3), the analogous decision problem becomes NP-complete (gallery entry konigsberg-oq-03), so the polynomial-time tractability of the r=2 case is genuinely special. For infinite graphs, the Erdős-Grünwald-Weiszfeld theorem (1936) characterizes which graphs admit one-way / two-way infinite Eulerian paths via finiteness of odd-vertex sets and connectivity conditions — the infinite path infrastructure (InfiniteWalk, BiInfiniteWalk) is formalized in konigsberg-oq-03-oq-02. Together, the trio (this entry for finite directed, konigsberg-oq-03 for hypergraph, konigsberg-oq-03-oq-02 for infinite) maps the boundary of where the degree-balance characterization extends.

sections.title: Directed Graph Basics
sections.summary: Defines DiGraph V (edges: Finset (V×V), noSelfLoops), outDegree, inDegree, IsBalanced, IsEulerianBalanced.
sections.mathContext: $\text{outDeg}(v) = |\{e \in E : e.1 = v\}|$. $\text{inDeg}(v) = |\{e \in E : e.2 = v\}|$. $\text{IsBalanced}(v)$: $\text{inDeg}(v) = \text{outDeg}(v)$.

sections.title: Directed Handshaking Lemma (Proved)
sections.summary: Proves sum_outDegree_eq_edgeCount and sum_inDegree_eq_edgeCount from first principles via double-counting (swap ∑_v ∑_e with ∑_e ∑_v). Derives sum_outDegree_eq_sum_inDegree by transitivity.

sections.title: Necessity: Eulerian Circuit Implies Balanced (Proved)
sections.summary: Defines HasEulerianCircuit with unique coverage (∃!) and step constraint. Three helper lemmas establish the bijection between walk positions and edges. Main theorem eulerian_circuit_implies_balanced proved: outDeg = source-count = target-count = inDeg, where middle equality uses the closed walk.
sections.mathContext: If $G$ has an Eulerian circuit with walk $[v_0,...,v_n]$ ($v_0 = v_n$), then $|\{i < n : v_i = w\}| = |\{i < n : v_{i+1} = w\}|$ for all $w$ (bijection: $i \mapsto i-1 \pmod{n}$). Combined with the edge-position bijection: $\text{outDeg}(w) = \text{inDeg}(w)$.

sections.title: Directed Eulerian Theorem and Path Characterization
sections.summary: Defines IsWeaklyConnected and HasEulerianPath. Axiomatizes directed_eulerian_iff (Hierholzer) and directed_euler_path_iff.
sections.mathContext: $G$ has an Eulerian circuit $\iff$ $\text{IsEulerianBalanced}(G)$ (weak connectivity required). $G$ has Eulerian path $s \to t$ $\iff$ $\text{outDeg}(s) = \text{inDeg}(s)+1$, $\text{inDeg}(t) = \text{outDeg}(t)+1$, and all others balanced.

sections.title: Concrete Examples
sections.summary: Defines directedTriangle (Fin 3, edges {(0,1),(1,2),(2,0)}) and directedPath (Fin 3, edges {(0,1),(1,2)}). Proves balance properties by native_decide.
sections.mathContext: Directed 3-cycle: all vertices balanced ($\text{in} = \text{out} = 1$). Directed path $0 \to 1 \to 2$: $\text{outDeg}(0) = 1 = \text{inDeg}(0)+1$, $\text{inDeg}(2) = 1 = \text{outDeg}(2)+1$, vertex 1 balanced.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.summary: Proves eulerian_balanced_sum_zero and eulerian_balanced_implies_degree_balance from the main theorem.
sections.mathContext: Eulerian circuit $\Rightarrow$ $\sum_v \text{outDeg}(v) = \sum_v \text{inDeg}(v)$ (as integers). Eulerian circuit $\Rightarrow$ $\text{inDeg}(v) = \text{outDeg}(v)$ for all $v$.

sections.title: Hierholzer Infrastructure: Greedy Trail and Circuit Existence
sections.summary: Develops the mathematical infrastructure for Hierholzer's directed Eulerian algorithm in 6 steps. (1) Open-walk counting (lines 419-504): for an open walk u→w (u≠w), target-count(w) = source-count(w)+1, plus the symmetric source-excess lemma. (2) maxTrail (lines 513-728): a greedy trail following outgoing edges, terminating since |E| decreases by 1 per step. (3) maxTrail_closed (lines 933-1041): in a balanced digraph, the greedy trail is always a closed circuit — proved via a 5-step balance contradiction (STEPs A-E). (4) circuit_exists + DirectedCircuit (lines 1052-1078): every non-empty balanced digraph contains a directed circuit. (5) remove_circuit_balanced (lines 1100-1107, sorry): removing a circuit preserves balance — the only sorry in the file, blocked on Finset.sdiff distributivity API. (6) euler_path_implies_degree_balance (lines 1125-1198, FULLY PROVED): Eulerian path implies asymmetric degree conditions at start/end. Five of the six steps are proved; only step 5 carries a sorry.
sections.mathContext: Key theorem: $G$ balanced + $G.edges \neq \emptyset$ $\Rightarrow$ $\exists$ directed circuit in $G$. Proof: run greedy trail from any vertex $v$ with an outgoing edge; by balance, the trail closes (proof by contradiction using open-walk counting). Removing the circuit preserves balance (each vertex appears equally often as trail source and target). The path-necessity step is the open-walk analogue: an Eulerian path $s \to t$ creates a +1 source asymmetry at $s$ and a +1 target asymmetry at $t$, while interior vertices remain balanced.

conclusion.summary: Formalizes the directed Eulerian theorem. Key proved results: directed handshaking lemma (∑ outDeg = |E| = ∑ inDeg, via double-counting), necessity direction for circuits (Eulerian circuit → balanced degrees, via walk position bijection and closed-walk degree balance), Hierholzer infrastructure (maxTrail + maxTrail_closed via 5-step balance contradiction, circuit_exists), and necessity direction for paths (euler_path_implies_degree_balance — fully proved, asymmetric +1/−1 at endpoints + interior balance). 25 of 26 theorems proved from first principles; 2 axioms (Hierholzer sufficiency and the full Eulerian path characterization) remain to be discharged; 1 sorry (remove_circuit_balanced, blocked on a Finset.sdiff distributivity step); 1202 lines.
conclusion.implications: The directed Eulerian theorem underpins de Bruijn sequence construction (a de Bruijn graph is Eulerian), DNA fragment assembly algorithms, and Eulerian circuit algorithms in network flow. The degree-balance characterization is also the basis for Hierholzer's O(|E|) directed Eulerian circuit algorithm.
openQuestions: Formalize Hierholzer's algorithm for constructing directed Eulerian circuits (eliminate directed_eulerian_iff axiom). The infrastructure is in place: circuit_exists builds one circuit; the remaining step is the splicing recursion, which requires remove_circuit_balanced (the file's only sorry) to recurse on the residual graph.

Discharge remove_circuit_balanced: the Finset.sdiff distributivity step needs $|E \setminus S \cap F| = |E \cap F| - |S \cap F|$ for $S \subseteq E$, which is straightforward once expressed in the right form.

Combine euler_path_implies_degree_balance (proved here) with a sufficiency direction to eliminate the directed_euler_path_iff axiom — the sufficiency direction reduces to circuit Eulerian theorem via the standard 'add the missing edge' trick: add $(t, s)$ to make $G$ balanced, find Eulerian circuit, remove $(t, s)$ to recover the Eulerian path.

Formalize de Bruijn sequences: B(n, Σ) is a directed graph on Σ^{n-1} with every vertex balanced (in = out = |Σ|), so the directed Eulerian theorem here guarantees Eulerian circuits, whose vertex sequences are exactly de Bruijn sequences.

Count Eulerian circuits via the BEST theorem: t_w(G) · ∏_v (outDeg(v)-1)! where t_w(G) is the number of arborescences rooted at w. This requires the Matrix-Tree theorem (Kirchhoff 1847) which is a separate substantial formalization effort.

references.title: Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis
references.venue: Commentarii academiae scientiarum imperialis Petropolitanae 8: 128-140 (presented 1735, published 1741)
references.note: The founding paper of graph theory. Euler proved the **necessity direction** of the Eulerian theorem for undirected graphs: a connected multigraph has an Eulerian circuit only if every vertex has even degree. Applied to the seven bridges of Königsberg (over the Pregel river, with two islands), Euler showed that no walk traversing each bridge exactly once and returning to its start can exist — because the four landmasses have degrees 3, 3, 3, 5 (all odd). The sufficiency direction (even degrees plus connectivity $\Rightarrow$ Eulerian circuit exists) was completed constructively by Hierholzer (1873, next reference). Euler's introduction of the abstract framework — vertices for landmasses, edges for bridges, ignoring all geometric data — marks the birth of *geometria situs* (geometry of position), the subject Poincaré would later rename *topology*. The directed analogue formalized in this Lean file (Eulerian circuit $\iff$ every vertex balanced, $\text{inDeg}(v) = \text{outDeg}(v)$) is the natural extension Euler did not consider but which follows the same necessity argument. The double-counting proof of the directed handshaking lemma ($\sum_v \text{outDeg}(v) = |E| = \sum_v \text{inDeg}(v)$) is the directed-graph version of Euler's $\sum_v \deg(v) = 2|E|$ identity for undirected graphs. English translation: 'The Solution of a Problem Relating to the Geometry of Position,' in N. L. Biggs, E. K. Lloyd, R. J. Wilson, *Graph Theory 1736-1936*, Oxford University Press 1976, pp. 3-8.

references.title: Ueber die Möglichkeit, einen Linienzug ohne Wiederholung und ohne Unterbrechung zu umfahren
references.venue: Mathematische Annalen 6(1): 30-32 (posthumous; written shortly before Hierholzer's death in 1871, edited for publication by Christian Wiener)
references.note: **Hierholzer's algorithm** — the first constructive proof of the *sufficiency* direction of the Eulerian theorem, completing the half left open by Euler 1736. Hierholzer (1840-1871, who died at 30 from typhus before publishing this work) gave the **splicing recursion**: start any closed walk in a connected graph with all-even degrees (such a walk must exist since outgoing edges are always available by the parity condition); if edges remain, find any vertex $v$ on the current walk with unvisited incident edges, run a sub-walk from $v$ back to $v$ in the residual graph (which is still all-even after removing the current walk's edges), and splice the sub-walk into the main walk at $v$; iterate until all edges are used. The algorithm runs in $O(|E|)$ time — linear in the number of edges — and applies *verbatim* to directed graphs with the balance condition $\text{inDeg}(v) = \text{outDeg}(v)$ at every vertex, which is the form axiomatized in this Lean file as `directed_eulerian_iff`. The infrastructure proved in this file's section 6 (lines 390-1198) — `maxTrail` (greedy trail), `maxTrail_closed` (closure under balance), `circuit_exists` (every non-empty balanced digraph contains a circuit) — supplies the first three of the four steps of Hierholzer's recursion; only the splicing step itself (which requires `remove_circuit_balanced`, the file's only `sorry`) remains to discharge the axiom and produce a fully verified constructive algorithm. Modern textbook treatment: D. B. West, *Introduction to Graph Theory*, 2nd ed., Prentice-Hall 2001, §1.2; original German online via the Göttinger Digitalisierungszentrum.

references.title: A Combinatorial Problem
references.venue: Proceedings of the Koninklijke Nederlandse Akademie van Wetenschappen (Series A) 49: 758-764
references.note: **De Bruijn sequences** — cyclic sequences over an alphabet $\Sigma$ in which every length-$n$ string over $\Sigma$ appears exactly once as a window. De Bruijn (and independently I. J. Good, *Journal of the London Mathematical Society* 21: 167-169, 1946 — discovered the same year) observed that such sequences correspond bijectively to **Eulerian circuits in the de Bruijn graph** $B(n, \Sigma)$: vertices are length-$(n-1)$ strings, directed edges are length-$n$ strings with edge $(w_1 \cdots w_{n-1}) \to (w_2 \cdots w_n)$ representing the window $w_1 \cdots w_n$. The de Bruijn graph is *regular* — every vertex has in-degree = out-degree = $|\Sigma|$ — and *weakly connected*, so the directed Eulerian theorem formalized in this Lean file (`directed_eulerian_iff`) guarantees Eulerian circuits exist, proving de Bruijn sequences of every order over every alphabet exist. The total number of distinct de Bruijn sequences of order $n$ over a binary alphabet is $|\Sigma|!^{|\Sigma|^{n-1}} / |\Sigma|^n = 2^{2^{n-1}-n}$ — a count established via the BEST theorem (next reference) applied to the de Bruijn graph. Modern algorithmic applications: pseudorandom number generation, cryptography (the binary de Bruijn sequence as a maximum-period sequence), and rotor positioning for combination locks. The de Bruijn graph connection establishes the Eulerian theorem proved in this file as a *foundational existence result* — Eulerian circuits are not merely a curiosity about Königsberg but the algorithmic engine behind a fundamental object in combinatorics.

references.title: Circuits and Trees in Oriented Linear Graphs
references.note: The **BEST theorem** (an acronym from de **B**ruijn, van Aardenne-**E**hrenfest, **S**mith, **T**utte — the latter two having proved a closely related result in their *Annals of Mathematics* paper 'On unicursal paths in a network of degree 4,' 1941, vol. 42, 1004-1010, and 'A ring in graph theory,' Cambridge Phil. Soc. 1947). The theorem gives the *exact count* of Eulerian circuits in a directed Eulerian graph: the number of distinct Eulerian circuits **starting at vertex $w$** equals $\mathrm{ec}(G, w) = t_w(G) \cdot \prod_{v \in V(G)} (\text{outDeg}(v) - 1)!$, where $t_w(G)$ is the number of **arborescences** (spanning directed trees with all edges oriented toward $w$, equivalently spanning *in-trees* rooted at $w$). Two remarkable consequences: (1) the count is *independent of the choice of starting vertex* $w$ up to the multiplicative factor $\text{outDeg}(w)$, since $t_w(G) \cdot \text{outDeg}(w)$ is symmetric in $w$ (this is sometimes stated as the *BEST identity* and follows from Markov chain reversibility); (2) the arborescence count $t_w(G)$ is computable via the **Matrix-Tree theorem** (Kirchhoff 1847, Tutte's generalization to directed graphs 1948) as a cofactor of the Laplacian matrix $L(G) = D - A$ where $D$ is the diagonal out-degree matrix and $A$ is the adjacency matrix. Cited in openQuestion #5 as the next layer beyond the qualitative existence result formalized in this file: where `directed_eulerian_iff` says 'Eulerian circuits exist iff balanced + weakly connected,' the BEST theorem says 'and there are exactly $\mathrm{ec}(G, w)$ of them.' A Lean formalization of the BEST theorem would require building the Matrix-Tree theorem first — a substantial but well-defined target.

references.title: Ueber die Auflösung der Gleichungen, auf welche man bei der Untersuchung der linearen Vertheilung galvanischer Ströme geführt wird
references.note: **Kirchhoff's Matrix-Tree theorem** — the foundational result of algebraic graph theory, proved by Gustav Kirchhoff at age 23 in the course of analyzing electrical circuits. The theorem states: for a finite undirected graph $G$ with Laplacian matrix $L(G) = D - A$ (where $D$ is the diagonal degree matrix and $A$ is the adjacency matrix), the number of **spanning trees** of $G$ equals *any cofactor* of $L(G)$ — equivalently, $\tau(G) = \frac{1}{n} \lambda_1 \lambda_2 \cdots \lambda_{n-1}$ where $0 = \lambda_0 < \lambda_1 \leq \cdots \leq \lambda_{n-1}$ are the eigenvalues of $L(G)$. Tutte (1948, *Proc. Cambridge Phil. Soc.* 44: 463-482) extended the theorem to *directed* graphs, proving that the number of arborescences rooted at vertex $w$ equals the $(w, w)$-cofactor of the *directed Laplacian* $L^\rightarrow(G) = D^\rightarrow - A$ where $D^\rightarrow$ is the diagonal out-degree matrix. **Connection to this Lean file**: the directed Matrix-Tree theorem is the engine behind the BEST theorem (previous reference) — counting arborescences $t_w(G)$ via Kirchhoff's cofactor formula yields the explicit Eulerian-circuit count $t_w(G) \cdot \prod_v (\text{outDeg}(v) - 1)!$ that openQuestion #5 envisions formalizing. Kirchhoff's original 1847 motivation was *physical*: by Ohm's law and the loop/node equations of a resistor network, the current distribution in an electrical network is governed by a linear system whose coefficient matrix is the graph Laplacian — and the determinantal structure of this matrix encodes the spanning-tree combinatorics. The flow-conservation interpretation cited in this file's keyInsight #9 (handshaking $\equiv$ Kirchhoff's current law) is *exactly* Kirchhoff's 1847 observation, making the directed handshaking lemma proved here the abstract combinatorial shadow of the physical conservation principle. English translation: in J. B. Biggs, E. K. Lloyd, R. J. Wilson, *Graph Theory 1736-1936*, OUP 1976, pp. 133-145.

references.title: An Eulerian path approach to DNA fragment assembly
references.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 98(17): 9748-9753
references.note: **The EULER assembler** — the landmark paper that introduced **Eulerian path-based DNA sequence assembly**, replacing the dominant Hamiltonian path approach (which is NP-hard) with the polynomial-time Eulerian approach (which the directed Eulerian theorem in this Lean file guarantees succeeds whenever the de Bruijn graph is connected and balanced). The pipeline: (1) shear the DNA into millions of short overlapping fragments (reads); (2) decompose each read into all length-$k$ substrings ($k$-mers); (3) construct the **de Bruijn graph** $B(k, \{A, C, G, T\})$ on the multiset of observed $k$-mers, with edge $(w_1 \cdots w_{k-1}) \to (w_2 \cdots w_k)$ for each observed $k$-mer $w_1 \cdots w_k$; (4) find an Eulerian path in this graph (existence guaranteed by the *directed* Eulerian theorem formalized here, with the balance and connectivity conditions automatic from the read coverage); (5) the consecutive $k$-mers along the Eulerian path *spell out* the assembled genome. Pevzner-Tang-Waterman's algorithm replaced the earlier Hamiltonian-path approach (Sanger-style assembly, used by Celera and the public Human Genome Project), reducing assembly complexity from NP-hard (Hamiltonian path) to $O(|E|)$ (Hierholzer's algorithm for Eulerian path). The breakthrough enabled **next-generation sequencing (NGS)**: Illumina's GAII (2007), HiSeq (2010), and NovaSeq (2017) platforms produce billions of short reads per run, and de Bruijn graph assemblers — Velvet (Zerbino-Birney 2008), SOAPdenovo (Li et al. 2010), SPAdes (Bankevich et al. 2012) — are now the standard pipeline for de novo genome assembly. The 1736 Königsberg bridge theorem of Euler — formalized in `konigsberg` and extended to digraphs in this file — thus reaches into 21st-century molecular biology as the *theoretical foundation* enabling whole-genome sequencing. Modern textbook reference: P. Compeau and P. Pevzner, *Bioinformatics Algorithms: An Active Learning Approach*, Active Learning Publishers, 3rd ed. 2018, Chapter 3.

Counting Eulerian Circuits: the BEST Theorem (van Aardenne-Ehrenfest, de Bruijn 1951; Smith, Tutte 1941–48). Once existence is established by directed_eulerian_iff (this file), the BEST theorem gives the exact count via arborescences and the Matrix-Tree theorem — the quantitative refinement of the qualitative result here.

Eulerian Paths in Hypergraphs and Infinite Graphs — generalizes the directed Eulerian theorem of this file along two orthogonal axes: (1) r-uniform hypergraphs for r≥3, where the analogous decision problem becomes **NP-complete**, sharply contrasting with the polynomial-time degree-balance characterization formalized here for r=2; and (2) infinite graphs, governed by the Erdős-Grünwald-Weiszfeld theorem (1936). The contrast quantifies the algorithmic specialness of the r=2 finite case proved here: the inDeg(v) = outDeg(v) vertex-local invariant has no analogue in higher dimensions or at infinity.

Infinite Paths in Graphs: ℕ-Indexed Formalization — provides the foundational infrastructure (InfiniteWalk, BiInfiniteWalk, IsEulerWalk with edge-injectivity, HasOneWayInfiniteEulerPath) for extending the directed Eulerian theorem of this file to infinite graphs. The closed-walk balance and walk-position bijections proved here for finite walks are the finite-graph base case; konigsberg-oq-03-oq-02's stream-equivalence and ℤ-indexed bi-infinite walks set up the Erdős-Grünwald-Weiszfeld characterization that the present file's finite degree-balance theorem cannot itself reach.

Euler's polyhedral formula V - E + F = 2 (Wiedijk #13) — Euler's *other* foundational graph-theory contribution (1758, building on the 1736 Königsberg paper that founded the field). The two results frame Euler's introduction of the abstract vertex-edge framework: Königsberg 1736 extracts global *existence* invariants from local vertex-degree parity; the polyhedral formula extracts global *topological* invariants (genus, the Euler characteristic χ = V - E + F) from local face-counting. The directed handshaking lemma proved here (∑ outDeg = |E| = ∑ inDeg) is the directed-graph analogue of the undirected handshaking identity ∑ deg(v) = 2|E| that underwrites Euler's polyhedral proof. Together the two entries anchor the *vertex-edge-arithmetic-yields-global-invariants* methodological pattern that defines classical graph theory.
